claims.text: Replacing TOR-TILD's EAM reference with a machine-learning interatomic potential trained on ab initio solid and liquid configurations near melting will improve reference–DFT phase-space overlap.
Improved phase-space overlap will reduce the thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to EAM-based TOR-TILD.
The target materials are equiatomic or near-equiatomic alloys containing at least five metals.
The intervention applies to both crystalline solid and disordered liquid states at approximately 0.85–1.0 times the melting temperature.
A Gaussian Approximation Potential or Moment Tensor Potential can be used as the thermodynamic-integration reference.
The machine-learning potential should be trained on a comprehensive set of ab initio configurations from both solid and liquid phases.
The machine-learning potential will capture diverse local atomic environments in both phases more accurately.
More accurate representation of local environments will align the reference potential-energy surface more closely with the ab initio potential-energy surface.
Training across solid and liquid configurations will reduce discrepancies between the machine-learning and DFT energy landscapes.
Reduced energy-landscape discrepancies will improve phase-space overlap.
Reduced energy-landscape discrepancies will shorten the thermodynamic-integration path.
The machine-learning reference is expected to reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch by approximately 30–50% relative to TOR-TILD's EAM references.
The machine-learning reference is expected to improve calculated free-energy accuracy.
TOR-TILD currently uses EAM reference potentials for thermodynamic integration of high-entropy alloys near melting.
The approach is primarily applicable to near-equiatomic alloys with at least five elements at temperatures close to melting.
The approach may be less effective in systems dominated by strong directional bonding or nonmetallic character.
The magnitude of mismatch reduction depends on the quality and breadth of the machine-learning training data.
The 30–50% mismatch-reduction estimate is preliminary.
The hypothesis is falsified if the machine-learning reference fails to reduce path mismatch by at least approximately 25% relative to EAM.
The hypothesis is falsified if the resulting free-energy deviation from the ab initio benchmark exceeds 10 meV/atom.
